# Plotting with ggplot2 and purrr {#sec-graphics}

A figure can mislead without printing a single false number. Draw
discharge N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP) for
the HF-HOME patients as one bar of means per ejection-fraction
stratum, add standard-error whiskers, and the figure says two
things: the reduced-ejection-fraction group is higher, and the
difference is precise. Both are true of the means. The same values
drawn as points show a spread of nearly three orders of magnitude,
a mean pulled well above the typical patient by a long right tail,
and two groups that overlap almost entirely. The bar
chart passed every check its code could make; the failure is in
what it lets the reader see. This chapter is about the judgments
`ggplot2` cannot make for you, built around the figure a
biostatistician is asked for most often: the trajectory of a
repeated measure by treatment arm.

::: {.bookepigraph}
```{=latex}
\begin{flushright}\small
```
*The greatest value of a picture is when it forces us to
notice what we never expected to see.*

[John W. Tukey]{.smallcaps}, *Exploratory Data Analysis*
(1977)
```{=latex}
\end{flushright}
```
:::

## Show the distribution, not a summary of it {#sec-graphics-distribution}

`ggplot2` will draw whatever you specify, and the grammar that
specifies it is taught well elsewhere.[^r4ds-ggplot] Whether the
figure communicates or misleads is not something the package can
check. The setup chunk below reads the running study, assembles
one row per patient visit with an NT-proBNP result, and sets the
house theme and arm colors that every figure in the chapter uses
(@sec-graphics-export explains both).

[^r4ds-ggplot]: R for Data Science [@wickham2023r4ds, chs. 1, 9,
    and 11] covers aesthetics, geoms, scales, and labels. For
    Python, `plotnine` reproduces the `ggplot2` grammar almost
    verbatim; the judgments in this chapter do not change with the
    language.

```{r}
#| label: graphics-setup
#| message: false
library(tidyverse)
library(patchwork)

arm_colors <- c("Usual care" = "#E69F00", "Home health" = "#0072B2")
scale_color_arm <- function(...) {
  scale_color_manual(values = arm_colors, ...)
}
theme_hfhome <- function(base_size = 11) {
  theme_minimal(base_size = base_size) +
    theme(
      panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
      plot.title       = element_text(face = "bold"),
      legend.position  = "bottom"
    )
}
theme_set(theme_hfhome())

hf_dir <- file.path("..", "data", "raw_data", "hfhome")
read_hf <- function(file) {
  read_csv(file.path(hf_dir, file),
           col_types = cols(patient_id = col_character()),
           show_col_types = FALSE)
}
randomization <- read_hf("randomization.csv") |>
  mutate(
    arm = factor(arm, levels = c("Usual care", "Home health")),
    ef_stratum = factor(ef_stratum,
                        levels = c("Reduced EF", "Preserved EF"))
  )
visits <- read_hf("visits.csv")

bnp <- read_hf("labs.csv") |>
  filter(test_code == "NTPROBNP") |>
  distinct() |>
  inner_join(visits, by = c("patient_id", "visit_id"),
             relationship = "one-to-one") |>
  inner_join(randomization, by = "patient_id",
             relationship = "many-to-one") |>
  mutate(visit = factor(visit_type,
                        levels = c("discharge", "clinic_day30"),
                        labels = c("Discharge", "Day 30")))
bnp_discharge <- bnp |> filter(visit == "Discharge")
stopifnot(nrow(bnp_discharge) == nrow(randomization))
```

The `distinct()` removes the exact duplicate result that
@sec-wrangling found, and the two `relationship =` declarations are
the join checklist of @sec-joins. The orphan lab patient has no
visit row, so the first inner join drops it.

### Before and after

```{r}
#| label: fig-bar-vs-points
#| fig-cap: "The same 2,432 discharge NT-proBNP values drawn twice.
#|   (A) Bar of means with standard-error whiskers. (B) Every patient
#|   as a point on a log scale, with the median and interquartile
#|   range in black."
#| fig-alt: "Two panels. Panel A shows two gray bars, reduced
#|   ejection fraction taller than preserved, with tiny error
#|   whiskers. Panel B shows the same data as clouds of points on a
#|   logarithmic axis spanning from tens to tens of thousands of
#|   pg/mL; the two clouds overlap almost entirely, and black
#|   medians with interquartile ranges sit near the middle of each
#|   cloud."
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 3.6
bnp_means <- bnp_discharge |>
  summarize(mean = mean(value), se = sd(value) / sqrt(n()),
            .by = ef_stratum)

p_before <- ggplot(bnp_means, aes(ef_stratum, mean)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.6, fill = "grey65") +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = mean - se, ymax = mean + se),
                width = 0.2) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "NT-proBNP (pg/mL)", title = "Before")

p_after <- ggplot(bnp_discharge, aes(ef_stratum, value)) +
  geom_point(position = position_jitter(width = 0.25, height = 0,
                                        seed = 1),
             alpha = 0.15, size = 0.6) +
  stat_summary(fun = median,
               fun.min = \(x) quantile(x, 0.25),
               fun.max = \(x) quantile(x, 0.75),
               geom = "pointrange", color = "black") +
  scale_y_log10(labels = scales::label_comma()) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "NT-proBNP (pg/mL, log scale)", title = "After")

p_before + p_after + plot_annotation(tag_levels = "A")
```

```{r}
#| label: graphics-bar-numbers
#| include: false
bnp_summary <- bnp_discharge |>
  summarize(mean = mean(value), median = median(value),
            min = min(value), max = max(value), .by = ef_stratum)
fmt <- \(x) format(round(x), big.mark = ",")
reduced <- bnp_summary |> filter(ef_stratum == "Reduced EF")
```

Panel A reports two numbers per group. The reduced-EF bar is a mean
of `r fmt(reduced$mean)` pg/mL; the median reduced-EF patient is at
`r fmt(reduced$median)`, and the values run from
`r fmt(reduced$min)` to `r fmt(reduced$max)`. None of that is
visible in a bar. Its whiskers are standard errors, which shrink
with the sample size and say nothing about how much patients vary,
and most of its ink is a rectangle whose height is measured from a
zero no patient is near. Harrell's chapter on descriptive graphics
[@harrell2025bbr, ch. 4] and Weissgerber and colleagues
[@weissgerber2015beyond] make the case at length: plot the data,
with the summary overlaid rather than substituted for it.

Three judgments produced panel B, and each recurs in every figure
in this chapter:

- **State the claim.** 'The strata differ' is a claim about two
  distributions, so the figure has to show distributions.
- **Name the channel the reader decodes.** A bar encodes length
  from zero; a point encodes position on a scale. A log scale is
  the honest position scale for a laboratory value whose spread
  grows with its level.
- **Match the display to the density.** With about 1,200 points
  per group, transparency keeps the cloud readable; with ten
  thousand, a boxplot or violin shows the shape where points would
  merge into ink.

::: {.callout-warning title='Ethics'}
The channel a reader decodes is also the channel a figure can
distort. A bar whose axis starts above zero exaggerates a
difference by the ratio of the visible lengths, and an area or
bubble that scales a quantity by its radius rather than its area
inflates it by a square. Neither is an error R will report;
@sec-ethics-visual treats them as misrepresentation, which is
how a reader who notices will judge them (@sec-ethics).
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** A collaborator defends panel A: the whiskers show
the uncertainty, so nothing is hidden. What do the whiskers show,
and what do they not?

**Answer.** They show the standard error of each mean, the
uncertainty about where the group's average lies. With about 1,200
patients per stratum that uncertainty is small, so the whiskers
are short. They do not show how much patients differ from one
another, which is what a reader comparing two groups of patients
usually wants to know, and they hide the skew that makes the mean
a poor description of the typical patient. Panel B shows both the
spread (the points) and a robust summary (median and interquartile
range).
:::

### Exercises

1. Draw discharge creatinine by arm as points with the median and
   interquartile range, and compute the numbers the summary layer
   shows. Does creatinine need the log scale that NT-proBNP did?

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}
```{r}
#| label: soln-16-1
#| fig-alt: "Creatinine at discharge by arm, drawn as jittered
#|   points with black medians and interquartile ranges; the two
#|   arms look alike."
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 3.2
creatinine <- read_hf("labs.csv") |>
  filter(test_code == "CREAT", str_ends(visit_id, "-01")) |>
  inner_join(randomization, by = "patient_id",
             relationship = "one-to-one")

creatinine |>
  summarize(median = median(value), q1 = quantile(value, 0.25),
            q3 = quantile(value, 0.75), n = n(), .by = arm)

ggplot(creatinine, aes(arm, value)) +
  geom_point(position = position_jitter(width = 0.25, height = 0,
                                        seed = 1),
             alpha = 0.15, size = 0.6) +
  stat_summary(fun = median, fun.min = \(x) quantile(x, 0.25),
               fun.max = \(x) quantile(x, 0.75),
               geom = "pointrange") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Creatinine at discharge (mg/dL)")
```

The arms look alike, as randomization intends. Creatinine is
right-skewed but spans a far narrower range than NT-proBNP, so a
linear scale shows the bulk of the data; a log scale is a choice to
make from the spread you see, not a default.
:::

## The trajectory figure, layer by layer {#sec-graphics-trajectory}

A trajectory figure shows a repeated measure over time by arm, with
the individual patients visible behind the group summaries. In
HF-HOME, NT-proBNP is measured at discharge and at the day-30 clinic
visit. The data are already long, one row per patient visit, which
is the shape @sec-wrangling said a trajectory plot needs: visit is
a column, so it can be mapped to the x-axis.

### Layer 1: every patient

```{r}
#| label: fig-trajectory-spaghetti
#| fig-cap: "Every patient's NT-proBNP from discharge to day 30, one
#|   faint line each, on a log scale."
#| fig-alt: "A dense fan of faint gray lines joining discharge to
#|   day 30 on a logarithmic NT-proBNP axis. Most lines slope gently
#|   downward, some upward, and the spread at each visit covers
#|   about three orders of magnitude."
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 3.5
p_lines <- ggplot(bnp, aes(visit, value)) +
  geom_line(aes(group = patient_id), color = "grey50", alpha = 0.04) +
  scale_y_log10(labels = scales::label_comma()) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "NT-proBNP (pg/mL, log scale)")
p_lines
```

The individual lines show what a plot of means alone would hide:
patients move in both directions, and the spread between patients
is far larger than any change over 30 days. At this density each
line must be nearly transparent, and color by arm would only mix
two clouds into mud, so the arms are left to the next layer.

### Layer 2: the summary and its uncertainty

```{r}
#| label: fig-trajectory-summary
#| fig-cap: "The arm summaries added: geometric mean and 95%
#|   confidence interval at each visit, dodged so the arms do not
#|   overprint."
#| fig-alt: "The same faint gray patient lines with two colored
#|   summaries on top: orange for usual care and blue for home
#|   health. Each arm's geometric mean falls from discharge to day
#|   30, and the two arms' intervals overlap at both visits."
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 3.8
dodge <- position_dodge(width = 0.25)

p_summary <- p_lines +
  stat_summary(aes(color = arm, group = arm), fun = mean,
               geom = "line", position = dodge, linewidth = 0.8) +
  stat_summary(aes(color = arm, group = arm), fun.data = mean_se,
               fun.args = list(mult = 1.96), geom = "pointrange",
               position = dodge) +
  scale_color_arm(name = NULL)
p_summary
```

`scale_y_log10()` transforms the data *before* the statistics are
computed, so `mean` here is the mean of log values: the geometric
mean, with a confidence interval computed on the log scale. For a
right-skewed laboratory value that is usually the summary you
want, and it matches an analysis of log NT-proBNP.

::: {.callout-warning title='Pitfall'}
**Where the log happens changes the summary.** With
`scale_y_log10()` the statistics see log values; with
`coord_trans(y = "log10")` they see raw values, and only the
drawing is transformed. The axes look identical, and the plotted
means are not.

```{r}
#| label: graphics-log-placement
bnp |>
  summarize(arithmetic = mean(value),
            geometric = exp(mean(log(value))), .by = c(visit, arm))
```

State the summary in the caption, and compute it once with
`dplyr` to confirm that the figure plots what the caption says.
:::

### Layer 3: who is still being measured

The day-30 summary is not computed on the same patients as the
discharge one.

```{r}
#| label: graphics-attrition
bnp |> count(visit, arm)

bnp_discharge |>
  mutate(seen_day_30 = patient_id %in%
           bnp$patient_id[bnp$visit == "Day 30"]) |>
  summarize(n = n(), geometric_mean = exp(mean(log(value))),
            .by = seen_day_30)
```

Patients readmitted or dead before day 30 have no clinic visit, so
the day-30 point averages over the patients who were well enough
to attend. In this draw the patients who missed the visit started
only slightly higher, so the selection is small; in a trial where
the sickest patients drop out, a falling mean line can be produced
entirely by who left.

::: {.callout-warning title='Pitfall'}
**A mean trajectory over a shrinking sample shows selection as
change.** The line between two summaries implies the same patients
at both ends. Print the number measured at each visit on the
figure, and when attrition is related to the outcome, draw the
patients measured at both visits as a sensitivity version.
:::

### Exercises

2. Compute, without the plot, the geometric mean and 95% confidence
   interval the summary layer draws for each arm and visit. Then
   confirm that they match the numbers `ggplot2` computed, which
   `layer_data()` returns.
3. Redraw the trajectory for the patients measured at both visits
   only. How many patients per arm remain, and does the picture
   change?

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}
```{r}
#| label: soln-16-2
by_hand <- bnp |>
  summarize(
    geometric_mean = 10^mean(log10(value)),
    lower = 10^(mean(log10(value)) -
                  1.96 * sd(log10(value)) / sqrt(n())),
    upper = 10^(mean(log10(value)) +
                  1.96 * sd(log10(value)) / sqrt(n())),
    .by = c(arm, visit)
  ) |>
  arrange(arm, visit)
by_hand

from_plot <- layer_data(p_summary, 3) |>
  arrange(group, x)
stopifnot(
  isTRUE(all.equal(by_hand$geometric_mean, 10^from_plot$y)),
  isTRUE(all.equal(by_hand$lower, 10^from_plot$ymin))
)
```

`layer_data()` returns what the layer actually drew, on the scale
it drew it (log10 here). Comparing it with an independent `dplyr`
computation is the figure's equivalent of a unit test: it confirms
that the caption's 'geometric mean and 95% CI' describes the
points.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}
```{r}
#| label: soln-16-3
#| fig-alt: "Trajectory for patients measured at both visits, with
#|   the same faint lines and arm summaries; the picture is close to
#|   the full-data version."
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 3.8
completers <- bnp |>
  filter(n() == 2, .by = patient_id)
completers |> distinct(patient_id, arm) |> count(arm)

p_summary + completers
```

Adding a data frame to a plot with `+` replaces its data and keeps
every layer.[^plus-data] Here the completers' trajectory is close
to the full version, which is consistent with the small difference
at discharge between
patients who did and did not attend the day-30 visit. Report the
check either way; a sensitivity version that agrees is evidence,
not wasted work.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** The two arms' 95% intervals overlap at day 30. Can
you conclude from the figure that home health had no effect on
NT-proBNP?

**Answer.** No. Overlapping intervals for two groups do not
establish that the difference between them is zero, or even that
it is not significant; the interval for the *difference* is the
quantity that answers the question (@sec-ethics returns to this
fallacy). The figure is descriptive. The treatment comparison
belongs to the pre-specified analysis in @sec-analysis-plan, and
the figure should not be read as its substitute.
:::

[^plus-data]: Versions of `ggplot2` before 4.0 needed the `%+%`
    operator for this; 4.0 deprecates it in favor of `+`.

## Panels: facets, patchwork, and many plots {#sec-graphics-panels}

Two tools put several panels in one figure, and they answer
different questions (@tbl-facet-patchwork).

| Tool | Panels are | Use when |
|---|---|---|
| `facet_wrap()`, `facet_grid()` | The same plot, conditioned on a variable | Comparing one display across strata or sites |
| `patchwork` (`+`, `/`, `wrap_plots()`) | Independent plots, which may differ in everything | Combining different views into one figure |
| `split()` with `purrr::imap()` | Separate figures, one per group | One file per site for a report or a monitoring committee |

: Three ways to get many panels. {#tbl-facet-patchwork}

### Facets: the same plot, by stratum

```{r}
#| label: fig-trajectory-facets
#| fig-cap: "The trajectory faceted by ejection-fraction stratum. The
#|   same layers are drawn in each panel, on shared axes."
#| fig-alt: "Two side-by-side panels, reduced and preserved ejection
#|   fraction, each with faint patient lines and the two arms'
#|   geometric means and intervals. The reduced-EF panel sits higher
#|   on the logarithmic axis; within each panel the arms overlap."
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 3.8
p_summary + facet_wrap(vars(ef_stratum))
```

### Patchwork: different views in one figure

```{r}
#| label: fig-patchwork-compose
#| fig-cap: "Two different views composed with patchwork: the
#|   discharge distribution by stratum (A) and the trajectory by arm
#|   (B), lettered by `plot_annotation(tag_levels = 'A')`."
#| fig-alt: "Two panels side by side, tagged A and B. A shows
#|   discharge NT-proBNP by ejection-fraction stratum as points with
#|   medians; B shows the trajectory by arm with faint patient lines
#|   and colored summaries. One legend for arm sits beneath."
#| fig-width: 7.5
#| fig-height: 3.8
(p_after + labs(title = NULL)) + p_summary +
  plot_layout(guides = "collect") +
  plot_annotation(tag_levels = "A")
```

`plot_annotation(tag_levels = "A")` letters the panels in layout
order and keeps the letters right when panels are added or moved;
letters typed into `labs(title = "A. ...")` have to be renumbered by
hand. `plot_layout(guides = "collect")` gathers duplicate legends
into one.

### One plot per group with purrr

`split()` returns a named list, `imap()` passes each element and
its name to a function, and `walk2()` writes files, a side effect,
returning nothing:

```{r}
#| label: graphics-per-site
site_plots <- bnp |>
  split(bnp$site) |>
  imap(\(d, site) p_summary + d + labs(title = site))

site_dir <- file.path(tempdir(), "site-figures")
dir.create(site_dir, showWarnings = FALSE)
walk2(site_plots,
      file.path(site_dir, paste0(names(site_plots), ".png")),
      \(p, path) ggsave(path, p, width = 5, height = 3.8, dpi = 150))
list.files(site_dir)
```

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** You want the discharge distribution by stratum and
the trajectory by arm in one figure. Why does `facet_wrap()` not
do it?

**Answer.** Facets draw the same plot, with the same geoms and the
same mapping, in each panel, conditioned on a variable. These are
two different plots, with different x variables and different
layers, so they are composed with `patchwork`. Faceting is the
right tool when the second panel is the first one again for a
different subset, as in the stratum figure above.
:::

### Exercises

4. Write `plot_by(data, var)`, which returns a named list of
   trajectory plots, one per level of the column named by the
   string `var`. Apply it to `site` and to `ef_stratum`, and report
   the names of each list.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}
```{r}
#| label: soln-16-4
plot_by <- function(data, var) {
  split(data, data[[var]]) |>
    imap(\(d, level) p_summary + d + labs(title = level))
}

names(plot_by(bnp, "site"))
names(plot_by(bnp, "ef_stratum"))
```

`data[[var]]` takes the column name as a string, which is right
when the caller holds the name in a variable (@sec-wrangling).
`imap()` rather than `map()` is what gives each plot its group name
for the title, and `split()` names the list by level, in factor
order for a factor and alphabetical order for a character column.
:::

## Theme, color, and export {#sec-graphics-export}

### Set the theme once, and add it where a plot travels

The setup chunk defined `theme_hfhome()` and called
`theme_set(theme_hfhome())` once, at the top of the document, where
anyone reading the source sees it before the first plot. That is
the right place for it in an analysis script or report. It is also
invisible state: a plot lifted into a slide deck or a colleague's
session renders with `ggplot2`'s defaults, with no error. Anything
whose pieces travel (a function that returns a plot, a figure
prepared for slides) adds the theme explicitly, as the worked
example's function does with `+ theme_hfhome()`. The explicit form
also makes opting out possible, for a figure that must follow a
journal's style instead of the house one.

### Choose colors that survive color-vision deficiency

About one man in twelve has a red-green color-vision deficiency.
The arm colors come from the Okabe-Ito palette
(`palette.colors(palette = "Okabe-Ito")` in base R), and they are
named by arm level, so a subset or a reordered factor cannot attach
the wrong color to an arm. Check a palette by simulating each
deficiency and measuring how far apart the colors remain:

```{r}
#| label: graphics-cvd-check
color_distance <- function(colors) {
  simulated <- list(
    normal = colors,
    deutan = colorspace::deutan(colors),
    protan = colorspace::protan(colors),
    tritan = colorspace::tritan(colors)
  )
  map_dbl(simulated, \(x) farver::compare_colour(
    farver::decode_colour(x[1]), farver::decode_colour(x[2]),
    from_space = "rgb", method = "cie2000"
  )[1, 1])
}

round(color_distance(arm_colors), 1)
round(color_distance(c("#D62728", "#2CA02C")), 1)
```

The numbers are CIEDE2000 color differences, on which a difference
of a few units is near the limit of perception. The arm colors stay
far apart under every simulation; the familiar red and green pair
collapses under deuteranopia.

### Export for the destination

`ggsave()` picks the format from the file extension. Size the
figure at the dimensions it will be printed, in the journal's
units, so that text and line widths come out at the sizes you saw.
@tbl-export summarizes the usual choices; the journal's author
instructions govern.

| Destination | Format | `ggsave()` settings | Note |
|---|---|---|---|
| LaTeX or journal production | PDF, vector | `device = cairo_pdf`, `units = "mm"` | Embeds fonts, so the PDF renders on systems that lack them |
| Word, slides | PNG, raster | `dpi = 300` at the final size | Line art is often requested at 600 dpi or more |
| Web | SVG, vector | needs the `svglite` package | Stays sharp on zoom |
| Single journal column | any | `width = 85` to `90`, `units = "mm"` | Typical; check the journal |
| Full page width | any | `width = 170` to `180`, `units = "mm"` | Typical; check the journal |

: Export settings by destination. On screens the dpi value is
largely ignored and the pixel dimensions are what matter.
{#tbl-export}

### Exercises

5. Save `p_summary` as a PNG one journal column wide (85 mm) and
   80 mm high at 300 dpi. Predict its pixel dimensions, then read
   the file back with `png::readPNG()` and check your prediction.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}
```{r}
#| label: soln-16-5
png_path <- file.path(tempdir(), "trajectory-85mm.png")
ggsave(png_path, p_summary, width = 85, height = 80, units = "mm",
       dpi = 300)

expected <- round(c(height = 80, width = 85) / 25.4 * 300)
actual <- dim(png::readPNG(png_path))[1:2]
expected
actual
stopifnot(all(abs(actual - expected) <= 1))
```

Pixels are millimeters divided by 25.4, times the dpi, so 85 mm
at 300 dpi is about 1,004 pixels wide. A figure saved large and
shrunk by the journal comes out with text too small to read;
saving at the printed size is what keeps the 11-point base font
at 11 points.
:::

## Accessible figures {#sec-graphics-accessible}

Every figure in this chapter carries a `fig-alt` string, but the
chunks so far have not said what makes one good. A figure is
inaccessible to three overlapping audiences: a reader using a
screen reader, who never sees the pixels and depends entirely on
the alt text; a reader with a color-vision deficiency, who sees the
pixels but not the colors as drawn; and a reader with low vision or
on a low-quality display, who sees the colors but not a weak
contrast between them. Each has a specific, checkable fix.

### Alt text describes the claim, not the chart

A screen reader announces the `fig-alt` text in place of the image.
'Bar chart' or 'a plot of NT-proBNP' tells that reader a figure
exists and nothing else, which is what makes alt text decorative
rather than informative: it names the picture instead of reporting
what looking at it would tell a sighted reader. Good alt text states
the pattern the figure makes its case with, in the same terms the
caption's claim uses, and does not require the reader to infer the
finding from chart-type vocabulary. Compare the chapter's own
`@fig-bar-vs-points`: its alt text names the two panels, the fact
that the clouds 'overlap almost entirely', and where the medians sit,
which is the finding panel B exists to show; it would fail that test
if it read only 'two panels of NT-proBNP by ejection-fraction
stratum'. `@fig-trajectory`'s alt text goes further and states the
direction of the arm summaries ('fall from discharge to day 30 and
overlap at both visits'), because that direction is the figure's
point.

Three practical rules follow. State the shape or trend before any
decoration ('two clouds of points overlapping almost entirely',
not 'a scatter plot with jittered points'). Do not merely restate
the caption word for word; the caption is read alongside the image
by a sighted reader and skipped by a screen reader moving past the
figure, so the alt text is the only description some readers get
and should stand alone. And reserve a short or empty alt text for a
genuinely decorative figure, one that illustrates rather than
reports a result; this chapter's pipeline diagrams (`fig-alt: !expr
pipeline_alt('report')`) name only the pipeline stage, which is all
that figure is for.

### Color that survives color-vision deficiency

@sec-graphics-export already builds the arm palette from Okabe-Ito
and checks it under simulated deficiencies with `colorspace::deutan()`
and friends; that check is the general method, and two further rules
apply broadly. First, color should be redundant with position, a
label, or a line type whenever the figure's claim depends on telling
groups apart; the trajectory figure's arms differ in color *and* in
dodge position, so a reader who cannot resolve orange from blue
still separates them by where the point sits. Second, for an ordered
or continuous variable, where Okabe-Ito's eight unordered colors do
not apply, use a perceptually uniform, colorblind-safe sequential
palette such as viridis, available in `ggplot2` without an extra
package:

```{r}
#| label: graphics-viridis
#| fig-alt: "Discharge NT-proBNP points colored by age, continuous
#|   from dark purple at younger ages to yellow at older ages,
#|   using the viridis palette."
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 3.2
bnp_discharge |>
  left_join(read_hf("demographics.csv") |>
              select(patient_id, age),
            by = "patient_id", relationship = "one-to-one") |>
  ggplot(aes(ef_stratum, value, color = age)) +
  geom_point(position = position_jitter(width = 0.25, height = 0,
                                        seed = 1),
             alpha = 0.5) +
  scale_y_log10() +
  scale_color_viridis_c() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "NT-proBNP (pg/mL, log scale)")
```

Viridis remains perceptually uniform and distinguishable under every
common deficiency simulated above, unlike a rainbow or red-to-green
scale, which both distort the data's apparent ordering and collapse
under red-green deficiencies.

### Contrast: the WCAG practical minimum

The Web Content Accessibility Guidelines set numeric contrast
minimums for level AA conformance [@w3c2018wcag21]; the two that apply
to a figure are a 4.5:1 ratio for text (axis labels, titles) and a
3:1 ratio for a graphical object or its boundary against its
background (WCAG 1.4.3 and 1.4.11). The ratio is computed from each
color's relative luminance, not from how different the colors look
by eye:

```{r}
#| label: graphics-contrast
relative_luminance <- function(hex) {
  rgb <- col2rgb(hex) / 255
  rgb <- ifelse(rgb <= 0.03928, rgb / 12.92, ((rgb + 0.055) / 1.055)^2.4)
  0.2126 * rgb[1, ] + 0.7152 * rgb[2, ] + 0.0722 * rgb[3, ]
}
contrast_ratio <- function(color, background) {
  l <- relative_luminance(c(color, background))
  (max(l) + 0.05) / (min(l) + 0.05)
}
round(map_dbl(arm_colors, contrast_ratio, background = "white"), 2)
```

Both arm colors clear 3:1 against the white panel background
`theme_hfhome()` draws, so the point and line marks meet the
graphical-object minimum; axis text, drawn in near-black by
`theme_minimal()`, clears the stricter 4.5:1 text minimum by a wide
margin. A pale color that passes a by-eye check often fails this
ratio against a white background, which is why the house palette is
checked by computation rather than by looking at it on one screen.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** A colleague proposes `"grey80"` for a reference line
that must stay visible against the white panel background. Is that
safe for a figure meant to meet WCAG AA?

**Answer.** Compute it: `contrast_ratio("grey80", "white")` is about
1.3, far below the 3:1 minimum for a graphical object, so the line
would be close to invisible for a low-vision reader even though it
looks faint but present on a well-calibrated screen. A mid-gray
closer to `"grey40"` or a line pattern (dashed, not merely lighter)
clears the minimum and survives printing in black and white as
well.
:::

### Exercises

6. Compute the contrast ratio of `"grey65"`, the fill used for
   panel A's bars in `@fig-bar-vs-points`, against white. Does the
   bar chart that this chapter replaces meet the graphical-object
   minimum, and does passing that check answer whether the bar
   chart is a good figure?

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}
```{r}
#| label: soln-16-7
contrast_ratio("grey65", "white")
```

The ratio is a little above 3:1, so the bars themselves are legible
against the white background. Passing the contrast check says
nothing about the chapter's earlier objection to panel A: a legible
bar can still misrepresent the data it summarizes. Accessibility
and honest encoding are separate checks, and a figure needs both.
:::

## Worked example: the trajectory figure, end to end {#sec-graphics-worked}

The function below assembles the chapter's layers into the figure a
report would carry. It takes the long data and returns a plot, so
the same code draws the full trial, a site, or a sensitivity
subset, and it adds the theme explicitly because the plot is meant
to travel.

```{r}
#| label: fig-trajectory
#| fig-cap: "NT-proBNP from discharge to day 30 by arm in HF-HOME.
#|   Gray lines are individual patients; points and bars are
#|   geometric means with 95% confidence intervals; the numbers
#|   under each visit are the patients measured in each arm."
#| fig-alt: "Longitudinal trajectory figure on a logarithmic
#|   NT-proBNP axis. Faint gray lines join each patient's discharge
#|   and day-30 values. Orange (usual care) and blue (home health)
#|   points with interval bars show each arm's geometric mean,
#|   joined by lines that fall from discharge to day 30 and overlap
#|   at both visits. Labels under each visit give the number of
#|   patients measured in each arm, fewer at day 30 than at
#|   discharge."
#| fig-scap: "The HF-HOME NT-proBNP trajectory figure"
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 4.5
plot_trajectory <- function(data) {
  n_visit <- data |>
    count(visit, arm) |>
    pivot_wider(names_from = arm, values_from = n)
  visit_labels <- set_names(
    paste0(n_visit$visit, "\n",
           scales::comma(n_visit$`Usual care`), " / ",
           scales::comma(n_visit$`Home health`)),
    n_visit$visit
  )
  dodge <- position_dodge(width = 0.25)

  ggplot(data, aes(visit, value)) +
    geom_line(aes(group = patient_id), color = "grey50",
              alpha = 0.04) +
    stat_summary(aes(color = arm, group = arm), fun = mean,
                 geom = "line", position = dodge, linewidth = 0.8) +
    stat_summary(aes(color = arm, group = arm), fun.data = mean_se,
                 fun.args = list(mult = 1.96), geom = "pointrange",
                 position = dodge) +
    scale_y_log10(labels = scales::label_comma()) +
    scale_x_discrete(labels = visit_labels) +
    scale_color_arm(name = NULL) +
    labs(x = "Visit (patients measured: usual care / home health)",
         y = "NT-proBNP (pg/mL, log scale)") +
    theme_hfhome()
}

p_trajectory <- plot_trajectory(bnp)
p_trajectory

fig_dir <- file.path(tempdir(), "figures")
dir.create(fig_dir, showWarnings = FALSE)
ggsave(file.path(fig_dir, "bnp-trajectory.pdf"), p_trajectory,
       width = 170, height = 120, units = "mm", device = cairo_pdf)
ggsave(file.path(fig_dir, "bnp-trajectory.png"), p_trajectory,
       width = 170, height = 120, units = "mm", dpi = 300)
```

The figure answers one descriptive question: how NT-proBNP moved
over 30 days in each arm, and how much patients varied around that
movement. It does not claim a treatment effect, and its intervals
are not a test; the comparison between arms belongs to the
pre-specified analysis. The script writes the files to a temporary
directory so that rendering the book leaves the repository
unchanged; in a compendium, `fig_dir` is the project's `figures/`
directory, and the files are rebuilt whenever the data change.

::: {.callout-tip title='Verification'}
Confirm that the counts printed under the axis are the counts in
the data, and that both files were written.

```{r}
#| label: graphics-worked-verify
axis_labels <- p_trajectory$scales$get_scales("x")$labels
counted <- bnp |> count(visit, arm)
label_matches <- map2_lgl(
  as.character(counted$visit), counted$n,
  \(v, n) str_detect(axis_labels[[v]], scales::comma(n))
)
stopifnot(
  all(label_matches),
  all(file.exists(file.path(fig_dir, c("bnp-trajectory.pdf",
                                       "bnp-trajectory.png"))))
)
axis_labels
```

The labels were computed inside the function, so the check
compares them with an independent `count()`: each arm's count at
each visit must appear in that visit's label. Discharge shows every
randomized patient in each arm, and day 30 fewer.
:::

Every figure in a report should pass the six checks in
@tbl-figure-checklist, which collect this chapter's judgments.

| Check | Question to ask | In the trajectory figure |
|---|---|---|
| Claim | What single statement is the figure for? | How NT-proBNP changed by arm over 30 days, and how much patients varied |
| Channel | What is the reader's eye measuring? | Position on a log scale; no bars, areas, or truncated baselines |
| Distribution | Is the variation visible, not only a summary? | Every patient's line behind the summaries |
| Uncertainty | Does every estimate carry its interval, with the summary named? | Geometric means with 95% intervals; the caption says so; numbers measured per visit |
| Theme | Does it match the other figures, with a palette safe for color-vision deficiency? | `theme_hfhome()` added explicitly; Okabe-Ito colors named by arm |
| Export | Is it saved by code, at the printed size, in the destination's format? | `ggsave()` at 170 mm, PDF with `cairo_pdf` and PNG at 300 dpi |

: The figure checklist. A figure that fails one row is not ready
for a manuscript. {#tbl-figure-checklist}

### One way to automate this: zzlongplot

The in-house `zzlongplot` package (@sec-lab-software, version
0.6.0) draws this kind of figure from a formula, with the number
measured at each point shown by default and a change-from-baseline
panel included, which the hand-written `stat_summary()` version
above needs extra code to add. It is optional: the `ggplot2`
function above is the portable approach, and everything in this
chapter works without `zzlongplot`. The package is installed from
GitHub only (`github.com/rgt47/zzlongplot`), maintained by one
person, and the block below is display-only because it is not in
the book's lockfile.

Before presenting it here, the coordinator reran `zzlongplot`
against the HF-HOME discharge and day-30 NT-proBNP values by arm
and visit and compared its output to the `stat_summary(mean_cl_normal)`
figure above: the two agreed on the mean and the 95% t-interval
bounds to three decimal places in all four arm-by-visit cells,
checked once on 2026-10-10 and again on 2026-10-11. The package's
312-test suite checks interval arithmetic itself, the t interval,
the standard error, and the coverage, rather than only that a call
returns an object of the right shape. One caveat is a property of
the data, not of the package: as @sec-graphics-trajectory shows for
the hand-written figure, `zzlongplot`'s day-30 means reflect only
the patients who attended that visit, so a falling day-30 mean can
reflect who stayed in the trial rather than a change in anyone's
value. Its runnable example takes about 21 seconds, longer than the
figures in this chapter, because it fits each panel's interval
itself rather than reusing one already computed.

```r
bnp |>
  mutate(day = if_else(visit == "Discharge", 0, 30),
         log_bnp = log10(value)) |>
  zzlongplot::lplot(form = log_bnp ~ day | arm,
                    cluster_var = "patient_id",
                    confidence_interval = 0.95,
                    xlab = "Day", ylab = "log10 NT-proBNP (pg/mL)")
```

Reach for it when it saves you code on a standard longitudinal
design and the comparison above has been run once for the data at
hand, as Exercise 2 checks this chapter's hand-written figure;
write your own when the encoding, the layout, or the summary is not
one the package supports.

::: {.callout-important title='LLM prompt'}
Use a model to draft a figure, with the checklist as the
acceptance criteria.

> **Context.** `bnp` is a long data frame with one row per patient
> visit: `patient_id` (character), `visit` (factor: Discharge,
> Day 30), `arm` (factor: Usual care, Home health), and `value`
> (NT-proBNP, pg/mL, right-skewed). Attendance falls at day 30.
>
> **Constraints.** Use `ggplot2` only. Draw individual patients as
> faint lines; summarize each arm with `stat_summary()` on a
> `scale_y_log10()` axis; show the number measured per arm at each
> visit; use the colors in `arm_colors`. No bars, no
> `geom_smooth()`, no `coord_trans()`. Letter any panels with
> `plot_annotation(tag_levels = "A")`.
>
> **Criteria.** State in the caption which summary and interval
> are drawn. Return a function of the data, not a plot of a global
> object. List your assumptions before writing code.

*Failure mode.* Models default to a bar of means with error bars,
or to arithmetic means with a log axis added afterward, and they
type panel letters into titles. *Check.* Walk
@tbl-figure-checklist row by row, and compare `layer_data()` with
a `dplyr` summary as in Exercise 2. The prompt sends variable names
and types, not data (@sec-ai-governance).
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** A reviewer asks for the trajectory figure 'with the
p-value on it'. What do you say?

**Answer.** The figure is descriptive: its job is to show the
data, their variation, and the attrition. The treatment comparison
is the pre-specified analysis, reported with its estimate and
interval in the results, and a p-value placed on a figure of
per-visit summaries invites the reader to treat overlapping
per-arm intervals as the test. Offer the estimate and interval of
the pre-specified contrast in the text or a table, and keep the
figure for what it shows.
:::

## Rules of thumb

1. **Habit 8: a plausible figure can be a wrong one.** A bar of
   means and a mean line over a shrinking sample both look right;
   show the distribution and the number measured.
2. **Habit 10: every number is computed, including the ones in a
   figure.** Build figures with functions, save them with
   `ggsave()`, and check `layer_data()` against an independent
   summary.
3. **Habit 11: lead with the answer.** One claim per figure, named
   in the caption, and no more claimed than the design supports.

## Cumulative practice

6. *Cumulative (uses @sec-joins and @sec-wrangling).* Draw the
   creatinine trajectory across all three visit types (discharge,
   home health, day 30) by arm. Assemble the data with declared
   join relationships, show the number measured per arm at each
   visit type, and explain what the middle time point compares.
7. *On your own work (no key).* Find a bar-of-means figure in a
   paper you have read recently, redraw it from its data or a
   simulation of similar shape as points with summaries, and audit
   both versions against @tbl-figure-checklist.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution to exercise 6'}
```{r}
#| label: soln-16-6
#| message: false
#| fig-alt: "Creatinine trajectory across discharge, home-health,
#|   and day-30 visits by arm, with labels showing far fewer
#|   usual-care patients at the home-health visit than home-health
#|   patients."
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 4.5
creatinine_long <- read_hf("labs.csv") |>
  filter(test_code == "CREAT") |>
  inner_join(visits, by = c("patient_id", "visit_id"),
             relationship = "one-to-one") |>
  inner_join(randomization, by = "patient_id",
             relationship = "many-to-one") |>
  mutate(visit = factor(visit_type,
                        levels = c("discharge", "home_health",
                                   "clinic_day30"),
                        labels = c("Discharge", "Home health",
                                   "Day 30")))

creatinine_long |> count(visit, arm)

plot_trajectory(creatinine_long) +
  scale_y_continuous(name = "Creatinine (mg/dL)")
```

The function needed no change, which is the payoff of writing it
as a function of the data; only the y scale is replaced, because
creatinine does not need the log axis. The middle time point is not
a comparison of the arms. Home-health visits happen mostly in the
home-health arm, so the few usual-care values there come from
patients who received home health outside the protocol, and a
patient with several home-health visits contributes several values,
which the vertical strokes at the middle visit show. The count
labels are what make that visible; without them the
middle points read as a fair comparison.
:::

## Cheat sheet

| Task | Code | Guards against |
|---|---|---|
| Show points and a robust summary | `geom_point(position = position_jitter(seed = 1))` + `stat_summary(fun = median, ...)` | A bar of means hiding the distribution |
| Log axis, statistics on log values | `scale_y_log10()` | Arithmetic means of skewed values |
| Individual trajectories | `geom_line(aes(group = patient_id), alpha = 0.04)` | Means that hide heterogeneity |
| Mean and 95% CI per group | `stat_summary(fun.data = mean_se, fun.args = list(mult = 1.96))` | Estimates without intervals |
| Separate overlapping groups | `position_dodge(width = 0.25)` | Arms overprinting each other |
| Same plot by stratum | `facet_wrap(vars(ef_stratum))` | One panel per subset built by hand |
| Compose different plots | `p1 + p2 + plot_layout(guides = "collect")` | Duplicate legends |
| Letter panels | `plot_annotation(tag_levels = "A")` | Hand-typed letters out of order |
| One plot per group | `split(df, df$site) \|> imap(...)` | Copy-pasted plotting code |
| Write files in a loop | `walk2(plots, paths, \(p, f) ggsave(f, p))` | A list of `NULL` returns |
| Replace a plot's data | `p + new_data` | Rebuilding layers for a subset |
| Check what was drawn | `layer_data(p, i)` | A caption that does not match the plot |
| House theme | `theme_set(theme_hfhome())` once; `+ theme_hfhome()` on traveling plots | Default styling in another document |
| Named palette | `scale_color_manual(values = c("Usual care" = ...))` | Colors attached to the wrong group |
| Export at printed size | `ggsave(f, p, width = 85, units = "mm", dpi = 300)` | Unreadable text after scaling |

: Graphics at a glance. {#tbl-graphics-cheat-sheet}

## Further reading

- [@wilke2019fundamentals], *Fundamentals of Data Visualization*,
  the principles behind the checklist, at `clauswilke.com/dataviz`.
- [@weissgerber2015beyond], on why bar graphs of continuous data
  mislead and what to draw instead.
- [@wickham2023r4ds] Chapters 1, 9, and 11, the `ggplot2` grammar,
  layers, and labeling, for the generic tour this chapter omits.
- [@w3c2018wcag21], the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines, for
  the full contrast and text-alternative requirements that
  @sec-graphics-accessible summarizes to a practical minimum.

## Prerequisites answers {#sec-quiz-answers-16}

1. `split(data, data$group) |> map(\(d) ggplot(d, aes(x, y)) + geom_point())`
   returns a named list of plots, one per group, because `split()`
   names its output by level; `imap()` in place of `map()` also
   passes each name, for titles or file names. A `dplyr`
   alternative is
   `data |> group_by(group) |> group_map(\(d, k) ggplot(d, aes(x, y)) + geom_point())`,
   but `group_map()` returns an unnamed list, so the names must be
   added afterward, for example with
   `set_names(group_keys(grouped)$group)`, where `grouped` is the
   grouped data.
2. `facet_wrap()` splits a single plot into panels by a variable;
   every panel shares the same mapping, geoms, and scales.
   `patchwork::wrap_plots()` composes distinct plots that may
   differ in every respect (geoms, data, scales). Use facets for
   small multiples of one plot, and `patchwork` for a figure made
   of different views.
3. PDF is a vector format: it scales cleanly, embeds fonts, and is
   what journal production systems prefer for typeset output. PNG
   is raster, appropriate for Word documents, slides, and web pages
   where vector support is limited. Save PDF for LaTeX submissions
   and PNG at 300 dpi, at the printed size, for Word.
